questions.q: What does idempotent mean, and why does it matter for APIs?
questions.a: An operation is idempotent when doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once. Networks fail in the middle of a request, so a client often cannot tell whether the server acted. If the operation is idempotent the client can simply retry.

questions.q: How would you make a POST that charges a card safe to retry?
questions.a: The client sends a unique idempotency key per intended operation. The server records the key under a unique constraint before doing the work and stores the result against it afterwards, in the same transaction as any local writes. The call to the card processor cannot join that database transaction, so the same key is passed on to the processor as well. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result; a concurrent repeat waits or gets a conflict.

questions.q: How long do you keep idempotency keys?
questions.a: Long enough to cover any realistic retry window, commonly 24 hours, then expire them to bound storage. State the window in the API documentation.

questions.q: A retry arrives while the first request is still running. What happens?
questions.a: The unique key makes the second insert fail or block. Either respond 409 so the client retries shortly, or wait for the first to finish and return its result. Never run the work twice.
